subtopic_detail: Three weeks of fever and weight loss with splinter haemorrhages in a man with a bioprosthetic aortic valve
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a sixty seven year old man with three weeks of fevers, drenching night sweats and a six kilogram weight loss. He has become breathless climbing the stairs at home over the past week.

He had a bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement four years ago and takes no anticoagulation. He had a dental extraction seven weeks ago. He has no intravenous drug use, no indwelling lines and no recent travel. Three sets of blood cultures were taken from separate sites before any antibiotic was given.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 104 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 95 per cent in room air, temperature 38.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge not documented previously, splinter haemorrhages in three nail beds, two tender nodules on the finger pulps, bibasal inspiratory crackles, spleen not palpable
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 102 g/L (130-180), white cell count 14.8 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C reactive protein 156 mg/L (less than 5), creatinine 118 micromol/L (60-110), urinalysis shows non visible haematuria, transthoracic echocardiogram reports a poorly visualised prosthetic valve with no definite vegetation, chest radiograph shows mild pulmonary congestion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat the transthoracic echocardiogram in one week and withhold antibiotics until a vegetation is demonstrated
options.rationale: Withholding treatment for a week in a man with a new regurgitant murmur, heart failure and this inflammatory picture risks valve destruction and systemic embolism. Imaging that has already failed to visualise a prosthetic valve is unlikely to succeed on repetition. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Start oral amoxicillin and arrange outpatient cardiology review once the blood culture results become available
options.rationale: Oral monotherapy does not achieve the sustained bactericidal concentrations needed to sterilise a vegetation, and prosthetic valve infection requires inpatient parenteral therapy. Outpatient management would also miss the haemodynamic deterioration already evident. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Arrange computed tomography of the chest abdomen and pelvis to search for an occult malignancy causing the fevers
options.rationale: Occult malignancy is a reasonable consideration in prolonged fever with weight loss, but it does not explain a new regurgitant murmur with peripheral embolic stigmata in a man with a prosthetic valve. Pursuing it first would delay treatment of the more likely and more urgent diagnosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Give a single dose of intravenous antibiotic and repeat the blood cultures four hours later to improve the yield
options.rationale: Cultures drawn after antibiotics have been started have a substantially reduced yield, which is why three sets were correctly taken beforehand. Deliberately culturing through treatment inverts the correct sequence. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Arrange transoesophageal echocardiography and start empirical intravenous antibiotics for prosthetic valve infection
options.rationale: A negative or non diagnostic transthoracic study does not exclude endocarditis, and transoesophageal imaging is required for a prosthetic valve because acoustic shadowing obscures the transthoracic view. Empirical parenteral therapy starts now because cultures are already taken and the clinical picture with a new murmur and heart failure will not tolerate delay. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Infective endocarditis is diagnosed using the modified Duke criteria, which combine major criteria of typical organisms in persistently positive blood cultures and evidence of endocardial involvement with minor criteria including predisposition, fever, vascular and immunological phenomena, and supportive microbiology. Three sets of blood cultures from separate venepuncture sites before antibiotics are the single most important investigation, because identifying the organism determines a treatment course measured in weeks. Transthoracic echocardiography is the initial imaging test but has a sensitivity of only around fifty to seventy per cent for native valves and considerably less for prosthetic valves, where acoustic shadowing obscures the view, so transoesophageal imaging is required when a prosthesis is present or when suspicion remains despite a negative study. Empirical therapy covers staphylococci, streptococci and enterococci and is adjusted once the organism is known. Indications for surgery include heart failure from valve dysfunction, uncontrolled infection with abscess or persistent bacteraemia, and recurrent embolism with a large mobile vegetation.
key_points: Three sets of blood cultures from separate sites before antibiotics are the key investigation
Transthoracic echocardiography is insensitive for prosthetic valves owing to acoustic shadowing
Transoesophageal imaging is required for any prosthetic valve or persisting clinical suspicion
A new regurgitant murmur with heart failure is both a diagnostic clue and a surgical indication
Surgery is indicated for heart failure, uncontrolled infection and recurrent embolism
explanation.pearls: Streptococcus gallolyticus, formerly Streptococcus bovis, endocarditis is associated with colonic neoplasia in a substantial proportion of cases, so isolating it obliges a colonoscopy even when the bowel history is entirely unremarkable.

subtopic_detail: Vomiting and hypotension in a woman on long term replacement who halved her dose during a diarrhoeal illness
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a forty four year old woman with two days of vomiting and light headedness. She has primary adrenal insufficiency diagnosed nine years ago and normally takes hydrocortisone twice daily with fludrocortisone each morning.

She developed diarrhoea three days ago and, worried about keeping food down, halved her hydrocortisone dose to make the tablets last. She has vomited four times today and has not kept down this morning's tablets. She has no abdominal pain, no fever and no urinary symptoms.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 82/48 mmHg lying with a fall to 64/40 mmHg on standing, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in room air, temperature 36.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, capillary refill three seconds, buccal and palmar crease pigmentation, abdomen soft and non tender with normal bowel sounds, no rash, alert and oriented
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 126 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 5.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), urea 12.4 mmol/L (2.5-8.0), creatinine 124 micromol/L (45-90), glucose 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-7.0), venous pH 7.30 (7.32-7.42), C reactive protein 8 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Take a random serum cortisol and a short synacthen test, withholding steroid until the results are available
options.rationale: Diagnostic testing is unnecessary in someone with an established diagnosis and would delay treatment in a life threatening presentation. Withholding steroid to preserve the validity of a test is the classic error in this scenario. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Restart her usual oral hydrocortisone dose with an antiemetic and observe her in the short stay unit overnight
options.rationale: Oral administration cannot be relied upon in a woman who has vomited four times and has not absorbed this morning's dose, and her usual dose is inadequate for an acute stress state. The parenteral route is required until vomiting settles. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Give intravenous fluids with insulin and dextrose to correct the hyperkalaemia before addressing the hypotension
options.rationale: The potassium and sodium disturbance here is a consequence of mineralocorticoid and glucocorticoid deficiency and corrects with hydrocortisone and saline. Treating the electrolytes as the primary problem addresses a symptom rather than the cause. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Give broad spectrum intravenous antibiotics for presumed sepsis and arrange blood cultures with a septic screen
options.rationale: She is afebrile with a C reactive protein of 8 mg/L and a clear precipitant in the form of dose reduction during a gastrointestinal illness. Antibiotics would treat a process for which there is no supporting evidence while the actual deficiency goes uncorrected. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Give intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg immediately with intravenous sodium chloride and glucose replacement
options.rationale: Hypotension with hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia in a woman who has reduced her replacement during illness is an adrenal crisis, treated with immediate parenteral hydrocortisone and volume resuscitation with isotonic saline. Treatment is given on clinical suspicion because delay carries a high mortality and the hydrocortisone dose also provides sufficient mineralocorticoid effect. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis is a preventable cause of death in people with known adrenal insufficiency, and most episodes follow a failure to increase replacement during intercurrent illness rather than a failure of diagnosis. The presentation combines hypotension resistant to fluids alone with hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia, and in primary disease is accompanied by hyperpigmentation from raised adrenocorticotrophic hormone. Treatment is immediate intravenous or intramuscular hydrocortisone with isotonic saline, given on suspicion without waiting for any confirmatory test in a patient with an established diagnosis. Sick day rules are the preventive counterpart and specify doubling the usual oral dose for fever or significant illness, and moving to parenteral hydrocortisone when vomiting or diarrhoea prevents reliable absorption. Every patient should carry a steroid emergency card, wear medical identification and hold an in date emergency hydrocortisone injection that they and a family member know how to use.
key_points: Most crises follow failure to increase replacement during illness rather than missed diagnosis
The picture is fluid resistant hypotension with hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and hypoglycaemia
Treat immediately with parenteral hydrocortisone and isotonic saline without awaiting any test
Sick day rules double the oral dose for fever and switch to parenteral for vomiting or diarrhoea
Patients need a steroid card, medical identification and an emergency injection kit they can use
explanation.pearls: Fludrocortisone can be omitted while a patient is receiving hydrocortisone at or above about 50 mg daily, because at that dose hydrocortisone provides sufficient mineralocorticoid activity on its own.

sources.label: Endocrine Society of Australia: Adrenal insufficiency

subtopic_detail: Plan to stop denosumab after four years of treatment in a woman whose bone density has normalised
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a seventy one year old woman who has received six monthly denosumab injections for four years after a wrist fracture from standing height. Her repeat bone density scan shows a lumbar spine T score improved from minus 2.8 to minus 1.6 and a femoral neck T score of minus 1.9.

She has had no further fractures. She tells you she is tired of injections, is pleased that her scan has improved and would like to stop treatment altogether. She takes calcium and vitamin D, walks daily and has no falls. She has no renal impairment and no dental problems.

data_table.Examination: Height 161 cm with no loss recorded over four years, body mass index 24 kg/m2, no kyphosis, no spinal tenderness, gait steady with normal tandem walking
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.38 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), 25 hydroxyvitamin D 78 nmol/L (greater than 50), creatinine 74 micromol/L with estimated glomerular filtration rate 72 mL/min/1.73m2, thyroid stimulating hormone and parathyroid hormone within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice?

options.text: Stop the denosumab now and repeat her bone density scan in two years to confirm that the gains have been maintained
options.rationale: Stopping without replacement therapy triggers a rebound increase in bone turnover with rapid loss of the density gained and a specific risk of multiple vertebral fractures. A two year scan would document the loss long after the fractures had occurred. (Source: Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management)

options.text: Stop the denosumab and commence calcium and vitamin D at higher doses with a supervised exercise programme
options.rationale: Calcium, vitamin D and exercise are useful adjuncts but have nothing like the antiresorptive potency needed to suppress the rebound turnover that follows cessation. They cannot substitute for a bisphosphonate in this situation. (Source: Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management)

options.text: Extend the dosing interval to twelve monthly injections as a way of gradually weaning her off the treatment
options.rationale: The antiresorptive effect of denosumab wanes after about seven months, so an extended interval produces the same rebound phenomenon in the gap between doses. Delaying a dose beyond the schedule is itself a recognised trigger for rebound fractures. (Source: Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management)

options.text: Continue denosumab indefinitely and explain that a normalised density scan is not a reason to reconsider treatment
options.rationale: Continuing is a legitimate option, but presenting it as the only one disregards a clearly expressed preference when a safe alternative exists. Her wish to stop injections can be accommodated with an appropriate transition rather than overruled. (Source: Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management)

options.text: Transition to a bisphosphonate starting around six months after her last injection rather than stopping outright
options.rationale: Denosumab is fully reversible, and stopping it without follow on therapy causes a rebound in osteoclast activity that produces rapid bone loss and a characteristic risk of multiple vertebral fractures within one to two years. Sequencing a bisphosphonate at the time the next injection would have fallen due preserves the gains while meeting her wish to stop the injections. (Source: Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management)

explanation.summary: Denosumab is a monoclonal antibody against receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa B ligand, given six monthly, and it produces greater bone density gains than bisphosphonates with good fracture reduction. Its defining pharmacological property is that the effect is entirely reversible and is not retained in bone, which contrasts with bisphosphonates that bind to hydroxyapatite and continue to act for years after the last dose. Consequently, stopping denosumab or even delaying a dose beyond about seven months releases a rebound surge in osteoclast activity, with rapid loss of accrued density and a well described risk of multiple spontaneous vertebral fractures. Anyone ceasing denosumab therefore requires follow on antiresorptive therapy, usually an oral or intravenous bisphosphonate commenced around the time the next injection would have been due. This makes adherence to the six monthly schedule a safety issue rather than a matter of convenience, and it is a key point to establish before the first injection is ever given.
key_points: Denosumab acts against receptor activator of nuclear factor kappa B ligand and is fully reversible
Unlike bisphosphonates it is not retained in bone, so the effect ends when dosing stops
Cessation or delay beyond about seven months triggers rebound bone loss and vertebral fractures
Follow on bisphosphonate therapy is required for anyone stopping denosumab
Adherence to the six monthly interval is a safety requirement rather than a convenience
explanation.pearls: A woman who misses a denosumab dose and presents at nine or ten months should have the injection given promptly and be specifically asked about new back pain, since rebound vertebral fractures are often multiple and can be clinically silent until height loss appears.

subtopic_detail: Unilateral effusion with a pleural protein of 34 and serum protein of 62 in a man taking diuretics for heart failure
stem:
You are the medical registrar seeing a seventy four year old man with three weeks of breathlessness on exertion. He has chronic heart failure with a reduced ejection fraction and takes frusemide, which was increased by his general practitioner a fortnight ago.

He has also lost four kilograms without trying and has a dry cough. He worked as a boilermaker in his twenties. He has no fever, no chest pain and no haemoptysis. A diagnostic pleural aspiration has been performed under ultrasound guidance.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92 beats per minute, blood pressure 128/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, SpO2 94 per cent in room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Stony dull percussion note with absent breath sounds over the right lower zone, trachea central, jugular venous pressure not elevated, no peripheral oedema, no clubbing, no palpable lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: Pleural fluid protein 34 g/L with serum protein 62 g/L, pleural lactate dehydrogenase 280 U/L with serum lactate dehydrogenase 420 U/L and a laboratory upper limit of normal of 250 U/L, pleural fluid glucose 4.2 mmol/L, pleural pH 7.38, no organisms on Gram stain, chest radiograph shows a moderate right sided effusion with no visible mass

lead_in: How should this fluid be interpreted and what should follow?

options.text: Transudate from cardiac failure, so increase the diuretic dose and repeat the chest radiograph in four weeks
options.rationale: Applying the criteria to these values gives a protein ratio of 0.55 and a lactate dehydrogenase ratio of 0.67, both above the thresholds that define an exudate. Treating it as cardiac failure also ignores the unilateral effusion with weight loss and an asbestos exposure history. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pleural disease)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pleural disease

options.text: Transudate that has been concentrated by diuresis, so withhold diuretics for a week and repeat the aspiration
options.rationale: Diuresis can raise the protein concentration of a cardiac transudate and occasionally push it across the threshold, which is a genuine pitfall, but the lactate dehydrogenase ratio is also raised and the clinical picture does not fit cardiac failure. Withholding diuretics would delay investigation of a likely malignant process. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pleural disease)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pleural disease

options.text: Exudate consistent with empyema, so insert an intercostal catheter and commence intravenous antibiotic therapy
options.rationale: Empyema is characterised by a pleural pH below 7.20, a low glucose, purulent fluid or positive microbiology, none of which are present. Draining and treating for infection would expose him to a procedure and antibiotics without indication. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pleural disease)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pleural disease

options.text: Exudate requiring further investigation, so arrange contrast computed tomography of the chest and cytological analysis
options.rationale: Both the protein ratio of 0.55 and the lactate dehydrogenase ratio of 0.67 exceed the thresholds, so this is an exudate and requires a cause to be identified rather than attributed to the heart. A unilateral exudate with weight loss and occupational asbestos exposure warrants contrast imaging and cytology to look for malignancy including mesothelioma. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pleural disease)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pleural disease

options.text: Indeterminate fluid, so calculate the serum to pleural albumin gradient and manage as cardiac failure if it exceeds 12
options.rationale: The albumin gradient is a useful adjunct when a patient on diuretics has a borderline result and the clinical picture genuinely suggests heart failure. Here the clinical picture points away from a cardiac cause, so a gradient result would not justify stopping the search. (Source: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pleural disease)
source_refs: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pleural disease

explanation.summary: Pleural fluid is separated into transudate and exudate because the distinction determines whether the cause lies in altered hydrostatic and oncotic pressures or in pleural pathology itself. Light's criteria classify fluid as an exudate if any one of three conditions is met, namely a pleural to serum protein ratio above 0.5, a pleural to serum lactate dehydrogenase ratio above 0.6, or a pleural lactate dehydrogenase above two thirds of the upper limit of the serum reference range. The criteria are highly sensitive for exudates but misclassify around a quarter of cardiac transudates in patients taking diuretics, because diuresis concentrates the protein, and in that specific situation a serum to pleural albumin gradient above 12 g/L supports a transudate. Transudates arise from heart failure, cirrhosis and nephrotic syndrome, while exudates arise from malignancy, infection, pulmonary embolism and inflammatory disease. A unilateral exudate with weight loss and asbestos exposure requires contrast imaging and cytology, and a negative cytology does not exclude mesothelioma.
key_points: Any one of the three Light's criteria being met classifies the fluid as an exudate
The thresholds are a protein ratio above 0.5, a lactate dehydrogenase ratio above 0.6, or fluid lactate dehydrogenase above two thirds of the serum upper limit
Diuretics concentrate protein and can misclassify a cardiac transudate as an exudate
A serum to pleural albumin gradient above 12 g/L supports a transudate in that situation
Unilateral exudate with weight loss and asbestos exposure requires imaging and cytology
explanation.pearls: Pleural fluid cytology is positive in only around sixty per cent of malignant effusions and considerably less in mesothelioma, so a negative result in a patient with asbestos exposure warrants local anaesthetic thoracoscopy rather than reassurance.

sources.label: Thoracic Society of Australia and New Zealand: Pleural disease

subtopic_detail: International normalised ratio of 8.4 with fresh melaena in a man on warfarin who started an antibiotic five days ago
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a seventy nine year old man who has passed three black tarry stools since last night and feels dizzy on standing. He takes warfarin for a mechanical mitral valve replacement and his control has been stable for years.

Five days ago he was prescribed trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole for a urinary tract infection by an after hours service. He takes no antiplatelet agent and no non steroidal anti inflammatory drugs. He has had no vomiting and no abdominal pain.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 112 beats per minute, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 per cent in room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Pale conjunctivae, melaena on rectal examination, abdomen soft and non tender, mechanical click audible on cardiac auscultation, no peripheral stigmata of chronic liver disease
data_table.Investigations: International normalised ratio 8.4 (target 2.5-3.5), haemoglobin 84 g/L (130-180) down from 138 g/L three months ago, platelets 232 x10^9/L (150-400), urea 14.2 mmol/L (2.5-8.0), creatinine 96 micromol/L (60-110), liver function tests within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management of his anticoagulation?

options.text: Withhold warfarin and recheck the international normalised ratio in 24 hours, giving red cell transfusion as needed
options.rationale: Simply omitting doses is appropriate for a raised reading without bleeding, but warfarin takes days to wear off and this man is actively bleeding with haemodynamic compromise. Waiting a day leaves him anticoagulated throughout the period of greatest risk. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Give oral vitamin K 5 mg and withhold warfarin, arranging endoscopy on the next available elective list
options.rationale: Oral vitamin K takes around twenty four hours to correct the reading and is used for a raised result without major bleeding. Neither the route nor an elective endoscopy timeline matches the urgency of major haemorrhage. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Give fresh frozen plasma at 15 mL/kg as the primary reversal agent alongside resuscitation and urgent endoscopy
options.rationale: Plasma contains the relevant factors at low concentration, so full reversal requires a large volume that risks fluid overload in an elderly man, and it corrects more slowly and less completely than the concentrate. It is reserved for when prothrombinex is unavailable. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

options.text: Give protamine sulfate with intravenous vitamin K and arrange urgent upper gastrointestinal endoscopy after transfusion
options.rationale: Protamine reverses heparin by binding it directly and has no effect whatever on warfarin, which acts by depleting vitamin K dependent clotting factors. It would delay effective treatment while providing no benefit. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

options.text: Give intravenous vitamin K with prothrombin complex concentrate, with resuscitation and urgent endoscopy alongside
options.rationale: Major bleeding on warfarin requires immediate and complete reversal, achieved by prothrombin complex concentrate which replaces the depleted factors within minutes, together with intravenous vitamin K which sustains the correction as the concentrate is consumed. Giving either alone leads to rebound anticoagulation or to delayed correction respectively. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Warfarin reversal is graded by whether bleeding is present and how severe it is, rather than by the international normalised ratio alone. A raised reading without bleeding is managed by withholding doses, with oral vitamin K added as the value climbs higher. Major bleeding, meaning bleeding that is life threatening, into a critical site, or causing haemodynamic compromise or a significant haemoglobin fall, requires immediate full reversal with prothrombin complex concentrate plus intravenous vitamin K. Both components are necessary because the concentrate restores factors within minutes but is consumed over roughly six to eight hours, while vitamin K takes six to twelve hours to act but sustains the correction. Antibiotics are a leading precipitant of unexpected over anticoagulation, particularly trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole, metronidazole and the macrolides, through cytochrome P450 inhibition and suppression of vitamin K producing gut flora.
key_points: Reversal strategy is determined by the presence and severity of bleeding, not by the reading alone
Major bleeding needs prothrombin complex concentrate plus intravenous vitamin K together
The concentrate acts within minutes but is consumed, while vitamin K sustains the correction
Protamine reverses heparin and has no effect on warfarin
Trimethoprim with sulfamethoxazole, metronidazole and macrolides commonly potentiate warfarin
explanation.pearls: In a patient with a mechanical mitral valve, full reversal creates a real thrombotic risk, so the plan for restarting anticoagulation is made at the time of reversal rather than left to the ward round several days later.

subtopic_detail: Worsening weakness with a forced vital capacity of 14 mL/kg two days after a pyridostigmine dose increase
stem:
You are the medical registrar called to the ward to see a sixty three year old woman with myasthenia gravis, admitted yesterday with increasing limb weakness and difficulty swallowing. Her pyridostigmine dose was increased two days ago by her neurologist over the telephone.

She has become weaker through the afternoon and now cannot lift her head from the pillow. She reports abdominal cramps and has had loose stools twice today. Her voice has become nasal and she has coughed twice while drinking water.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 58 beats per minute, blood pressure 134/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, SpO2 95 per cent in room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Bilateral ptosis, weak neck flexion against gravity, proximal limb weakness worse on repetition, pupils constricted at 2 mm, skin moist with visible salivation, fine fasciculations over the deltoids, single breath count of 12
data_table.Investigations: Forced vital capacity 14 mL/kg having been 22 mL/kg this morning, venous carbon dioxide 44 mmHg (41-51), chest radiograph clear, potassium 4.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), C reactive protein 6 mg/L (less than 5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Increase the pyridostigmine dose further and reassess her strength after the next dose has taken effect
options.rationale: The cholinergic features of miosis, salivation, cramps, diarrhoea, bradycardia and fasciculations indicate excess rather than insufficient cholinesterase inhibition. Increasing the dose would deepen the depolarising block and the secretion load. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Administer an edrophonium test at the bedside to distinguish myasthenic from cholinergic weakness before acting
options.rationale: Edrophonium testing risks precipitating profound weakness, bradycardia and asystole in a patient who may already be cholinergic, and it is no longer used in this situation. The decision does not need to wait for a diagnostic manoeuvre with that risk profile. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Commence high dose oral prednisolone and arrange plasma exchange to begin on the ward the following morning
options.rationale: Immunotherapy is central to treating a myasthenic crisis but works over days, and high dose corticosteroid characteristically worsens weakness transiently in the first one to two weeks. Neither addresses a vital capacity that has fallen by a third in a single day. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Give supplemental oxygen by face mask to maintain saturations above 94 per cent and repeat the vital capacity overnight
options.rationale: Oxygen corrects the saturation while masking progressive ventilatory failure, since saturations are preserved until very late in neuromuscular respiratory compromise. Relying on oximetry here would allow decompensation to occur unobserved. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Withhold pyridostigmine and transfer to intensive care for airway protection and ventilatory support assessment
options.rationale: A forced vital capacity of 14 mL/kg with bulbar weakness and a falling single breath count indicates impending respiratory failure requiring critical care regardless of which crisis is operating, and the cholinergic features mean the anticholinesterase should be held rather than escalated. Withholding pyridostigmine also resolves the diagnostic question over the following hours without a hazardous bedside test. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Myasthenic crisis is respiratory failure from weakness of the diaphragm, intercostal or bulbar muscles, and it is precipitated by infection, surgery, pregnancy, tapering of immunotherapy, or drugs including aminoglycosides, macrolides, fluoroquinolones, beta blockers and magnesium. Cholinergic crisis, now rare because pyridostigmine is dosed more conservatively, arises from excess anticholinesterase and produces weakness accompanied by muscarinic features of miosis, salivation, lacrimation, bradycardia, abdominal cramps and diarrhoea, along with fasciculations. Distinguishing them matters for the drug decision, but the airway decision is identical and is made on respiratory parameters. Forced vital capacity and negative inspiratory force are the measures that matter, with intubation usually considered as vital capacity approaches 15 mL/kg or about one litre, because oxygen saturation remains normal until immediately before collapse. Definitive treatment of a myasthenic crisis is plasma exchange or intravenous immunoglobulin with corticosteroid, noting that steroids commonly worsen weakness transiently before helping.
key_points: Forced vital capacity and single breath count guide airway decisions, not oxygen saturation
Intubation is considered as vital capacity approaches 15 mL/kg or about one litre
Miosis, salivation, bradycardia, cramps and fasciculations indicate cholinergic excess
Edrophonium testing is hazardous in this setting and is no longer used to discriminate
Plasma exchange or immunoglobulin is definitive, while corticosteroids may worsen weakness initially
explanation.pearls: Magnesium sulfate impairs acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction and can precipitate a myasthenic crisis, so a woman with myasthenia who develops pre eclampsia needs an alternative anticonvulsant strategy planned in advance with neurology.

subtopic_detail: Facial oedema with eosinophilia and a rising creatinine four weeks after starting an anticonvulsant
stem:
You are the medical registrar seeing a fifty two year old woman with a widespread rash and fever. She was started on carbamazepine four weeks ago for trigeminal neuralgia and has taken no other new medication.

The rash began on her trunk five days ago and has spread to her limbs. Her husband says her face looks swollen. She feels generally unwell with aching and has had no diarrhoea and no cough. She has no history of atopy or drug allergy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 102 beats per minute, blood pressure 122/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in room air, temperature 38.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Confluent morbilliform eruption over trunk and limbs affecting about sixty per cent of body surface, marked periorbital and facial oedema, no mucosal erosions, no blistering, Nikolsky sign negative, tender cervical and axillary lymphadenopathy
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 16.4 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0) with eosinophils 1.9 x10^9/L (less than 0.5) and atypical lymphocytes on film, alanine aminotransferase 268 U/L (less than 35), creatinine 142 micromol/L (45-90) from a baseline of 72, C reactive protein 68 mg/L (less than 5), blood cultures negative at 24 hours

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Continue carbamazepine with an oral antihistamine, treating this as a self limiting morbilliform drug eruption
options.rationale: A simple morbilliform eruption does not produce fever, facial oedema, eosinophilia and organ involvement, and continuing the drug in this syndrome prolongs and worsens the reaction. The systemic features are precisely what separate the two. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions

options.text: Cease carbamazepine and treat as toxic epidermal necrolysis with transfer to a specialised burns unit for care
options.rationale: Epidermal necrolysis produces painful skin with blistering, mucosal erosions and a positive Nikolsky sign, none of which are present here, and it does not typically cause eosinophilia. Misclassifying the reaction would direct her to the wrong unit and the wrong supportive care. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions

options.text: Continue carbamazepine and commence intravenous antibiotics for a presumed systemic bacterial infection with rash
options.rationale: Blood cultures are negative and the eosinophilia with atypical lymphocytes and facial oedema is not a bacterial pattern, so antibiotics would treat an unsupported diagnosis. Adding a new drug class during a severe hypersensitivity reaction also risks confusing the culprit. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions

options.text: Cease carbamazepine immediately, commence systemic corticosteroid and monitor liver renal and thyroid function
options.rationale: Fever with facial oedema, a widespread eruption, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia with atypical lymphocytes and hepatic and renal involvement two to eight weeks after an aromatic anticonvulsant describes drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms. Stopping the culprit is essential, systemic corticosteroid is used for significant organ involvement, and prolonged monitoring is needed because relapse and late autoimmune thyroid disease are both characteristic. (Source: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions)
source_refs: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions

options.text: Cease carbamazepine and substitute phenytoin to maintain control of her facial pain while the rash settles
options.rationale: Phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbitone and lamotrigine are aromatic anticonvulsants with well documented cross reactivity in this syndrome, so substituting one for another risks perpetuating the reaction. A structurally unrelated agent would be required. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

explanation.summary: Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms is a severe delayed hypersensitivity reaction distinguished from ordinary drug eruptions by its latency, its systemic features and its organ involvement. The latency of two to eight weeks is longer than most drug reactions, which is a frequent reason the culprit is overlooked. Characteristic features are fever, a widespread morbilliform or oedematous eruption, facial oedema, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia with atypical lymphocytes, and involvement of liver, kidney, lung or heart. The commonest culprits are aromatic anticonvulsants, allopurinol, sulfonamides, vancomycin and minocycline, and human herpesvirus 6 reactivation is implicated in its pathogenesis and in its tendency to relapse. Mortality is around ten per cent, usually from hepatic failure or myocarditis, and treatment is prompt withdrawal of the drug with systemic corticosteroid for significant organ involvement and a slow taper over weeks.
key_points: Latency is two to eight weeks, longer than most drug eruptions, so the culprit is often overlooked
Facial oedema, eosinophilia with atypical lymphocytes and organ involvement define the syndrome
Aromatic anticonvulsants, allopurinol, sulfonamides and vancomycin are the usual culprits
Aromatic anticonvulsants cross react, so one cannot be substituted for another
Mortality is around ten per cent, chiefly from hepatic failure or myocarditis
explanation.pearls: Autoimmune thyroid disease develops in a minority of patients two to six months after apparent recovery from this syndrome, so thyroid function is rechecked at three and six months even when the rash and liver tests have fully normalised.

sources.label: Australasian College of Dermatologists: Severe cutaneous adverse reactions

subtopic_detail: Sodium rising from 108 to 126 over fifteen hours in a malnourished woman on thiazide who was volume deplete
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a sixty one year old woman admitted overnight with confusion and one generalised seizure. She takes a thiazide diuretic for hypertension, drinks around forty standard drinks a week and eats poorly.

She received two 100 mL boluses of 3 per cent sodium chloride in the emergency department for the seizure, which terminated, followed by 0.9 per cent sodium chloride running at 125 mL/hour overnight. She has passed 2.8 litres of urine since midnight. She is now awake, oriented and asking for breakfast.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 82 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 per cent in room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Moist mucous membranes, jugular venous pressure visible at 3 cm, no peripheral oedema, no ascites, body mass index 18 kg/m2, no focal neurological deficit, normal speech and comprehension
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 126 mmol/L (135-145) having been 108 mmol/L on admission fifteen hours ago, potassium 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), magnesium 0.62 mmol/L (0.70-1.10), urea 3.1 mmol/L (2.5-8.0), urine osmolality now 92 mOsm/kg having been 480 mOsm/kg on admission, thyroid function and morning cortisol within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue the saline infusion at the current rate, since her sodium remains below the lower reference limit
options.rationale: The concern is no longer the absolute value but the speed of the rise, which has already been 18 mmol/L in fifteen hours against a recommended limit of 8 mmol/L in twenty four hours. Continuing saline while she autocorrects would push the overshoot further. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Give a further 100 mL bolus of 3 per cent sodium chloride to protect against a recurrence of her seizure
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is reserved for active severe symptoms, and she is now awake, oriented and neurologically normal. Giving more would accelerate a correction that is already dangerously fast. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Commence tolvaptan to control the rate of rise and correct the residual hyponatraemia in a more controlled fashion
options.rationale: Vasopressin receptor antagonists promote free water excretion and therefore raise sodium further, which is the opposite of what is needed. They are also contraindicated where overly rapid correction is a concern. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Stop the saline, give 5 per cent glucose with desmopressin and recheck the sodium every two hours to relower it
options.rationale: Correcting the volume depletion switched off her vasopressin, producing a water diuresis that is driving an overshoot, evidenced by a urine osmolality that has fallen to 92 mOsm/kg and 2.8 litres of urine output. Relowering with electrolyte free water and desmopressin to stop the diuresis is the established approach when the twenty four hour limit has been exceeded in someone at high risk of osmotic demyelination. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Restrict fluid to one litre daily and repeat the electrolytes in the morning before making any further changes
options.rationale: Fluid restriction treats a dilutional hyponatraemia from excess antidiuretic hormone and does nothing to halt a brisk water diuresis that is already raising the sodium too quickly. Waiting until morning allows many more hours of uncontrolled rise. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: In chronic hyponatraemia the brain adapts by extruding organic osmolytes, and correcting the sodium faster than the brain can regain them causes osmotic demyelination syndrome, which appears days later as dysarthria, dysphagia, quadriparesis or a locked in state and is frequently irreversible. Australian practice therefore limits correction to no more than 8 mmol/L in twenty four hours, with a stricter limit of 4 to 6 mmol/L in those at highest risk, namely people with alcohol use disorder, malnutrition, hypokalaemia, liver disease or a sodium below 105 mmol/L. The specific trap is hypovolaemic hyponatraemia, where volume repletion removes the hypovolaemic stimulus to vasopressin release and unleashes a water diuresis that raises the sodium rapidly without further intervention. A sudden increase in urine output with a falling urine osmolality is the warning sign, and it can be anticipated rather than merely detected. When the limit has been exceeded, relowering with electrolyte free water and desmopressin is recommended, and desmopressin can also be used proactively to clamp the diuresis while correction proceeds at a controlled rate.
key_points: Correct chronic hyponatraemia by no more than 8 mmol/L in twenty four hours
Use a stricter 4 to 6 mmol/L limit with alcohol use, malnutrition, hypokalaemia or sodium below 105
Volume repletion switches off vasopressin and unleashes a water diuresis that overcorrects
A rising urine output with falling urine osmolality is the warning sign of impending overshoot
Relowering with glucose and desmopressin is indicated when the limit has been exceeded
explanation.pearls: Replacing potassium in a hyponatraemic patient raises the serum sodium independently of any sodium given, because potassium entering cells displaces sodium outwards, so potassium replacement must be counted in the day's correction budget.

subtopic_detail: Pulmonary oedema and a blood pressure of 230/130 forty minutes after a beta blocker given for episodic palpitations
stem:
You are the medical registrar called urgently to a ward where a forty eight year old man has deteriorated. He was admitted this morning for investigation of six months of episodic headache, palpitations and drenching sweats, during which his blood pressure has been recorded between 190/110 and 230/125 mmHg, settling to normal in between.

Forty minutes ago the covering resident prescribed oral metoprolol for a pulse of 130 beats per minute. He is now acutely breathless, sitting bolt upright and coughing pink froth. He has no history of ischaemic heart disease and an echocardiogram two weeks ago showed a structurally normal heart with preserved systolic function.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 126 beats per minute, blood pressure 230/130 mmHg, respiratory rate 36 breaths per minute, SpO2 84 per cent on fifteen litres per minute via reservoir mask, temperature 37.4 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Cool mottled peripheries with a pale diaphoretic face, widespread inspiratory crackles to the apices, pink frothy sputum, jugular venous pressure raised at 6 cm, no murmur audible over the respiratory noise
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram shows sinus tachycardia with lateral ST depression and no ST elevation, high sensitivity troponin 148 ng/L (less than 14), creatinine 118 micromol/L (60-110), glucose 12.4 mmol/L (3.5-7.0), plasma free metanephrines requested on admission and still pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Give intravenous phentolamine and start a sodium nitroprusside infusion with intensive care involvement
options.rationale: The episodic triad with paroxysmal severe hypertension points to catecholamine excess, and the deterioration within forty minutes of a beta blocker is characteristic of unopposed alpha stimulation, in which loss of beta two mediated vasodilatation leaves alpha vasoconstriction unchecked and precipitates crisis with pulmonary oedema. Reversing the alpha blockade deficit with phentolamine, supported by a titratable vasodilator, treats the actual mechanism. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Give a further dose of intravenous metoprolol to control the tachycardia driving the pulmonary oedema
options.rationale: Additional beta blockade deepens the unopposed alpha vasoconstriction that produced the crisis and further impairs an already failing ventricle. This is the specific intervention that converts a paroxysm into a life threatening event. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Give intravenous frusemide and morphine and arrange urgent coronary angiography for a presumed acute coronary event
options.rationale: The troponin rise reflects demand ischaemia and catecholamine mediated myocardial injury rather than plaque rupture, and treating the pulmonary oedema alone leaves the driving vasoconstriction untouched. Angiography would not address the mechanism and delays definitive treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Give intravenous labetalol as a combined alpha and beta blocking agent to lower the pressure in a balanced way
options.rationale: Labetalol blocks beta receptors several times more potently than alpha receptors, so in catecholamine excess it behaves functionally like a beta blocker and can worsen the crisis. Its combined action is not balanced enough for this situation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Start a glyceryl trinitrate infusion alone and titrate it against the blood pressure while awaiting the biochemistry
options.rationale: Nitrate reduces preload and helps the pulmonary oedema but does not overcome the intense alpha mediated vasoconstriction, so the pressure will remain dangerously high. Waiting for pending biochemistry before definitive treatment is not tenable at this blood pressure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Phaeochromocytoma and paraganglioma are catecholamine secreting tumours that classically present with the triad of episodic headache, palpitations and sweating on a background of paroxysmal or sustained hypertension, though the full triad is present in a minority. Diagnosis rests on plasma free metanephrines or twenty four hour urinary fractionated metanephrines, which are more sensitive than catecholamines because metabolism to metanephrines occurs continuously within the tumour rather than only during secretory episodes. The cardinal management principle is that alpha blockade must precede beta blockade, conventionally with phenoxybenzamine or prazosin for ten to fourteen days before surgery, with a beta blocker added only afterwards for reflex tachycardia. Giving a beta blocker first removes beta two mediated vasodilatation while leaving alpha mediated vasoconstriction unopposed, precipitating hypertensive crisis, pulmonary oedema and myocardial injury. Around forty per cent of cases are associated with a germline mutation, so all patients are referred for genetic assessment regardless of family history.
key_points: Plasma free metanephrines outperform catecholamines because tumour metabolism is continuous
Alpha blockade always precedes beta blockade, typically for ten to fourteen days before surgery
Beta blockade first removes beta two vasodilatation and leaves alpha vasoconstriction unopposed
Phentolamine is the short acting alpha antagonist used to rescue an unopposed alpha crisis
About forty per cent of cases carry a germline mutation, so all patients need genetic referral
explanation.pearls: Catecholamine excess can produce a takotsubo pattern of apical ballooning with a troponin rise and unobstructed coronary arteries, so a stress cardiomyopathy picture in someone with paroxysmal hypertension should prompt metanephrine testing rather than reassurance after a normal angiogram.
